Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |

    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same

references:

author: Clankerusecase

detection:

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446") or SHA1 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446") or MD5 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446") or SHA1 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446") or MD5 in~ ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0b
status: experimental

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.file_hash IN ("a68dd1e6a6e35ec3771e1f94fe796f55dfe65a2b94560516ff4ac189390dfa1c", "fb5c97557230a27460fdab01fafcfabeaa49590bafd5b6ef30501aa9e0a51142", "783b4019fc5b942a29846132d28441c8fc31bed8", "b06b126b9e26af03a7ef2f8b8e90d446")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.file_name, Filesystem.file_hash
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

Outbound egress to node-ipc stealer infrastructure (azurestaticprovider[.]net / 37.16.75.69) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects network connections to attacker-owned exfiltration infrastructure used by the malicious node-ipc 9.1.6 / 9.2.3 / 12.0.1 npm packages published 14 May 2026. Any host reaching these atoms after package install should be treated as a credential-theft incident. Rationale: Pivots on two atomic IOCs explicitly named in the Snyk advisory (37.16.75.69 and azurestaticprovider.net), each independently corroborated by StepSecurity and Upwind. No expected legitimate traffic to either atom — attacker-owned exfil infrastructure. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/node-ipc-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.upwind.io/feed/malicious-node-ipc-npm-package-credential-theft • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/stealer-backdoor-found-in-3-node-ipc.html
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1195.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Researcher / red-team sandbox intentionally detonating a node-ipc IOC sample
  • Threat-intel platform validating IOC reachability from an enrichment sensor
  • Internal honeypot or canary host instrumented to call known-bad domains for SOC training
  • DNS-over-HTTPS resolver logs caching previous lookups when no real connection was made
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","detonator","sentinel-ti-","honeypot") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("thor.exe","loki.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): On any hit, immediately enumerate the initiating process tree (InitiatingProcessFileName + parent) — confirm whether the originating process is node.exe / node and which package directory was loaded. Pull `npm ls node-ipc` and lockfile contents from the host. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the device, block 37.16.75.69 and *.azurestaticprovider.net at egress, kill the offending node process, and revoke ALL credentials accessible from that environment (npm tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS keys, SSH, kubeconfig, GCP service accounts, Terraform state, shell-history-resident secrets). Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the firing host's outbound connections for the prior 7 days to surface staging/recon connections; sweep CI runners and developer laptops for the affected node-ipc versions and for the related UCs (DNS lookups, __ntw=1 marker, nt-* temp dirs).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "37.16.75.69"
   or RemoteUrl has_any ("azurestaticprovider.net","sh.azurestaticprovider.net")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true

    or DestinationHostName has "azurestaticprovider.net"
    or RequestURL has "azurestaticprovider.net"

(ImNetworkSession
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DstIpAddr == "37.16.75.69"
    or DstHostname has "azurestaticprovider.net"
    or Url has "azurestaticprovider.net"
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstHostname, DstPortNumber, Url, EventProduct)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DNS lookup for azurestaticprovider[.]net node-ipc exfil domain AICommand & Control High
Surfaces hosts resolving the attacker-controlled domain azurestaticprovider.net (or sh.azurestaticprovider.net) used by the malicious node-ipc payload, even when the subsequent TCP egress is firewall-blocked. DNS-layer pivot catches hosts that loaded the package but did not complete exfiltration. Rationale: DNS pivot catches the same campaign at an earlier layer than TCP egress and survives proxy-level blocks. Domain is unique to this campaign and referenced verbatim in StepSecurity, Upwind, and Snyk advisories. ContextImageFileName lets the analyst confirm node.exe / npm as the requesting process. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/node-ipc-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.upwind.io/feed/malicious-node-ipc-npm-package-credential-theft
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel enrichment sensor doing IOC reachability checks
  • DNS server forwarding cache-warmup queries from another resolver
  • Security researcher / SOC analyst running curl/dig from a jump host
  • RPZ logging shows blocked queries — confirms detection efficacy, not malicious activity
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("ti-enrich-","sandbox-","honeypot-"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify the requesting process via ContextImageFileName / InitiatingProcessFileName — confirm node.exe / npm / yarn / pnpm as parent and pull the host's package-lock.json for node-ipc versions 9.1.6 / 9.2.3 / 12.0.1. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole or RPZ-block *.azurestaticprovider.net at the resolver, isolate any developer/CI host where the lookup originated, rotate all credentials reachable from that environment (npm, GitHub, AWS, SSH, kube, Terraform state, GCP). Step 3 (hunt): Cross-reference against UC1 (TCP egress) to see whether exfiltration completed; if no TCP follow-on the credentials may still be unexposed — but assume compromise. Sweep the org for additional node-ipc installs via npm/yarn/pnpm lockfile inventory.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "azurestaticprovider.net"
   or RemoteUrl endswith ".azurestaticprovider.net"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Hits=count(),
            SampleProc=any(InitiatingProcessFileName),
            SampleCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
            SampleUser=any(InitiatingProcessAccountName)
            by DeviceName, RemoteUrl
| order by FirstSeen asc
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where Name has "azurestaticprovider.net"
 | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, ResultCode),
(ImDnsActivity
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where DnsQuery has "azurestaticprovider.net"
 | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, DnsResponseCodeName, EventProduct)
| order by TimeGenerated asc

node-ipc stealer __ntw=1 environment marker in process command line AIInstallation High
Hunts for the __ntw=1 environment-variable marker reportedly used by the malicious node-ipc payload to signal that a child has already inherited the stealer context (preventing re-entry). Presence of this token in any process or child command-line is a high-fidelity indicator the payload executed on the host. Rationale: `__ntw=1` is a campaign-specific environment marker called out verbatim in the Snyk advisory and corroborated by StepSecurity — no mainstream npm package or build tool uses this token. Single-string match on CommandLine works because env vars set inline (e.g. `__ntw=1 node ...`) and parent-spawned children with that prefix surface in EDR command-line telemetry. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/node-ipc-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.upwind.io/feed/malicious-node-ipc-npm-package-credential-theft
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1027 T1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher / IR analyst reproducing the malware on a sandbox
  • Internal threat-hunt query stored in an analyst's shell history that gets re-exec'd
  • Sigma/test harness firing a synthetic event with the literal IOC for tuning
  • Documentation file or README opened in an editor whose telemetry surfaces __ntw=1 in the process arglist of a grep/findstr
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox-","detonator-","malware-rev-") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("grep.exe","findstr.exe","rg.exe","sigma-cli"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the full process tree around the hit — parent (likely node.exe / npm / yarn / pnpm), command line, and SHA256. Confirm whether node_modules/node-ipc/node-ipc.cjs exists on the host and what version is recorded in package-lock.json or yarn.lock. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the node process tree, quarantine the affected package directory, and rotate every credential category named in the advisory (npm, GitHub PAT/SSH, AWS / Azure / GCP, kubeconfig, Terraform state, ~/.bash_history-resident secrets, AI/dev-tool API keys). Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all hosts in the org for the same IOC, then pivot to UC1/UC2 (egress + DNS) for the same host's prior 7 days to confirm exfiltration completion.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "__ntw=1"
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "__ntw=1"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImProcessCreate
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "__ntw=1"
    or ParentProcessCommandLine has "__ntw=1"
    or TargetProcessCommandLine has "__ntw=1"
 | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentProcessCommandLine, TargetProcessCommandLine, EventProduct),
(SecurityEvent
 | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
 | where EventID == 4688
 | where CommandLine has "__ntw=1" or ParentProcessName has "__ntw=1"
 | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, ProcessId)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Malicious node-ipc package landed on disk under node_modules AIDelivery Medium
Hunts for file-system writes of node-ipc.cjs into any node_modules/node-ipc/ directory after the 14 May 2026 publication window, surfacing developer workstations, CI runners, build containers, and artifact registries that installed a candidate-malicious release. Pair with version triage (9.1.6 / 9.2.3 / 12.0.1). Rationale: Anchors on the exact CommonJS file Snyk identifies as malicious (`node-ipc.cjs`) and the canonical install path (`node_modules/node-ipc/`). Time-bound to the publication window so analysts only see installs that could be the bad versions. Hunting tier because a hit alone does not prove the version is malicious — needs package.json/lockfile triage as Step 1. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/node-ipc-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.upwind.io/feed/malicious-node-ipc-npm-package-credential-theft • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/stealer-backdoor-found-in-3-node-ipc.html
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer installing a still-uncompromised legacy version (e.g. 12.0.0) after the cutoff
  • CI cache warmup writing node-ipc into a build container from a private mirror with safe versions
  • Docker image layer-extraction surfacing node-ipc.cjs writes from older base images
  • Local node_modules vendoring during yarn/pnpm migrations (massive file-create bursts that include node-ipc)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Read the sibling `package.json` (`FolderPath/../package.json`) on each host and confirm version. Versions 9.1.6, 9.2.3, 12.0.1 = malicious; anything else = downgrade or pin. Step 2 (contain): On confirmed malicious version — isolate the host, delete the affected node_modules tree, clear the npm/yarn/pnpm cache, refresh the lockfile pinning to a safe version, and treat all credentials accessible from that environment as exposed. Step 3 (hunt): Inventory ALL artifact registries (Artifactory, Nexus, internal npm proxy), CI cache volumes, ephemeral build worker images, and Docker layers for the same file; pivot to UC1/UC2/UC3 on each candidate host.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp >= datetime(2026-05-14T00:00:00Z)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName =~ "node-ipc.cjs"
| where FolderPath has "node_modules" and FolderPath has "node-ipc"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp asc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated >= datetime(2026-05-14T00:00:00Z)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreate")
| where TargetFileName =~ "node-ipc.cjs"
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules" and TargetFilePath has "node-ipc"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated asc
title: Malicious node-ipc CommonJS Bundle Written Under node_modules (May 2026)
id: c41a83d7-2e0b-4f6a-90ef-7d8b1c2a5e09
description: Detects creation/modification of node_modules/node-ipc/node-ipc.cjs after 14 May 2026, the publication date of the malicious 9.1.6, 9.2.3, and 12.0.1 releases.
references:
  - https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-node-ipc-versions-published-npm/
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/node-ipc-npm-supply-chain-attack
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/19
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1195.002
  - attack.command_and_control
  - attack.t1105
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_name:
    TargetFilename|endswith:

  condition: selection_name
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate install of a non-malicious node-ipc version; triage by reading the parent package.json version field
level: medium

(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 (@TargetFilename:*\\node_modules\\node-ipc\\node-ipc.cjs OR @TargetFilename:*/node_modules/node-ipc/node-ipc.cjs)) OR (source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:PATH @file.path:*/node_modules/node-ipc/node-ipc.cjs)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| regex("(/|\\\\)node_modules(/|\\\\)node-ipc(/|\\\\)node-ipc\\.cjs$", field=TargetFileName, flags=i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName, UserName], function=min(@timestamp))
| _time >= 1747180800000
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as proc values(Filesystem.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="node-ipc.cjs" AND Filesystem.file_path="*node_modules*node-ipc*" AND Filesystem.action="created" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where firstTime >= relative_time(now(),"-30d@d") AND firstTime >= strptime("2026-05-14T00:00:00","%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.process_name) as proc values(Filesystem.user) as user from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="node-ipc.cjs" AND Filesystem.file_path="*node_modules*node-ipc*" AND Filesystem.action="created" by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where firstTime >= relative_time(now(),"-30d@d") AND firstTime >= strptime("2026-05-14T00:00:00","%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S") | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
node.js process staging credential dump in nt-* temp directory AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the staging artefact the malicious node-ipc payload writes — a temp directory matching `$TMPDIR/nt-*` populated by a node process — used to compress harvested SSH / cloud / kube / GitHub / Terraform / shell-history credentials before exfil. Catches the campaign at the collection layer even if egress is firewall-blocked. Rationale: Combines two campaign-specific behaviours from the Snyk advisory: (a) the temp directory prefix `nt-` and (b) a node process as the writer. Threshold of ≥3 distinct files per directory suppresses single-file noise while still firing on the credential-dump fan-out (90+ categories). Catches the campaign at the collection step even when egress is blocked. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/node-ipc-npm-supply-chain-attack • https://www.upwind.io/feed/malicious-node-ipc-npm-package-credential-theft
ATT&CKT1074.001 T1552.001 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Node.js test framework (e.g. some Jest/Mocha snapshot tooling) writing nt-prefixed scratch files
  • Node.js native build (node-gyp) using temp scratch directories during compile
  • Electron app's installer/updater extracting nt-prefixed temp artefacts on Windows
  • A developer running a CLI tool whose temp prefix happens to begin with 'nt'
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("node-gyp","electron-builder","jest","mocha") or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("npm.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe") and DistinctFiles < 10)
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the file inventory inside the matching nt-* directory — confirm presence of files resembling credential artefacts (id_rsa, .aws/credentials, kubeconfig, .gitconfig, .npmrc, .terraformrc, .bash_history). Check the writing process tree for node-ipc on disk. Step 2 (contain): Kill the node process, isolate the host, preserve the nt-* directory for forensics, and rotate every credential the host had access to (treat as fully compromised; the staging dir confirms collection occurred). Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to UC1/UC2 (azurestaticprovider.net + 37.16.75.69 egress) on the same host to determine whether the stage was exfiltrated; sweep CI runners for the same staging pattern.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath matches regex @"(?i)([\\/]Temp[\\/]nt-|/tmp/nt-|/var/folders/.+?/T/nt-)"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp),
            DistinctFiles=dcount(FileName), SampleFiles=make_set(FileName, 25),
            TotalBytes=sum(FileSize)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FolderPath
| where DistinctFiles >= 3
| order by FirstSeen asc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node.exe","node")
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where TargetFilePath matches regex @"(?i)([\\/]Temp[\\/]nt-|/tmp/nt-|/var/folders/.+?/T/nt-)"
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), DistinctFiles=dcount(TargetFileName),
            SampleFiles=make_set(TargetFileName, 25), TotalBytes=sum(TargetFileSize)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, EventProduct
| where DistinctFiles >= 3
| order by FirstSeen asc
title: Node.js Process Writes to nt-* Temp Directory (node-ipc Stealer Staging)
id: f0c5e842-9a16-4a3d-b71e-2c0d8e5fa317
description: Detects a Node.js process creating files in a temp directory matching the nt-* prefix reportedly used by the malicious node-ipc 9.1.6 / 9.2.3 / 12.0.1 payload to stage harvested credentials before exfiltration.
references:
  - https://snyk.io/blog/malicious-node-ipc-versions-published-npm/
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/node-ipc-npm-supply-chain-attack
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/19
tags:
  - attack.collection
  - attack.t1074.001
  - attack.credential_access
  - attack.t1552.001
logsource:
  category: file_event
detection:
  selection_image:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '/node'
  selection_path:
    TargetFilename|contains:
      - '\Temp\nt-'
      - '/tmp/nt-'
      - '/T/nt-'
  condition: selection_image and selection_path
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate Node.js tooling that happens to use an nt- prefix for scratch files (rare)
level: medium

(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe) (@TargetFilename:*\\Temp\\nt-* OR @TargetFilename:*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\nt-*)) OR (source:linux.auditd @process.name:node (@file.path:/tmp/nt-* OR @file.path:/var/folders/*/T/nt-*))
#event_simpleName=FileWritten
| ContextImageFileName=/[\\\\/]node(\\.exe)?$/i
| regex("([\\\\/]Temp[\\\\/]nt-|/tmp/nt-|/var/folders/.+?/T/nt-)", field=TargetFileName, flags=i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ContextImageFileName], function={
    distinct_count := count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true)
  })
| distinct_count >= 3
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_name) as files dc(Filesystem.file_name) as file_count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Temp\\nt-*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/tmp/nt-*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/var/folders/*/T/nt-*") AND Filesystem.process_name IN ("node.exe","node") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where file_count >= 3 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Filesystem.file_name) as files dc(Filesystem.file_name) as file_count from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where (Filesystem.file_path="*\\Temp\\nt-*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/tmp/nt-*" OR Filesystem.file_path="*/var/folders/*/T/nt-*") AND Filesystem.process_name IN ("node.exe","node") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.process_name Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where file_count >= 3 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

FrostyNeighbor PicassoLoader drop to %AppData%\WinDataScope\Update.js AIInstallation High
Hunts the article-specific second-stage drop: a JavaScript PicassoLoader payload written to a fixed AppData subfolder ('WinDataScope') used by FrostyNeighbor's March 2026 Ukrtelecom-themed compromise chain. The folder name and filename are both fingerprinted by ESET against multiple samples in this campaign. Rationale: WinDataScope is a folder name nowhere referenced in legitimate software inventories — ESET fingerprints it directly to FrostyNeighbor's PicassoLoader staging in the May 2026 report. Combined with the file name Update.js this is a near-zero-FP file-write signature. Cross-checked against: • https://cert.gov.ua/article/40240 • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1010/ • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/
ATT&CKT1027.009 T1036.005

  • Threat intel detonation labs writing the IOC to disk
  • Backup software restoring an archived Update.js artifact
  • Security researcher repository clone containing this sample

| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsMpEng.exe","MpCmdRun.exe") and InitiatingProcessAccountName =~ "system")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Hash the file (SHA-1/256) and compare to ESET's published B65551D339AECE718EA1465BF3542C794C445EFC and E15ABEE1CFDE8BE7D87C7C0B510450BAD6BC0906; pull the parent process tree (expect wscript.exe with --update arg). Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host via Defender Live Response or Falcon Network Containment; kill any wscript.exe/cscript.exe running Update.js; remove the WinDataScope folder and any scheduled tasks referencing it. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep org for additional WinDataScope folders, any DNS lookups to needbinding.icu / nebao.icu / algsat.icu / sardk.icu / alexavegas.icu / lavanille.buzz, and ViberPC.dll image loads.

FrostyNeighbor JS dropper self-relaunch with --update flag AIExploitation High
Detects the FrostyNeighbor first-stage JavaScript dropper's documented self-relaunch pattern: wscript.exe / cscript.exe executes a .js file with the literal '--update' argument so the second branch of the script can install PicassoLoader. The flag string is bespoke to this campaign and is not used by legitimate Windows Script Host workflows. Rationale: The article explicitly states the first-stage script re-executes itself with the --update flag to branch into the PicassoLoader drop. The double-dash --update form is uncommon in WSH-launched JavaScript and pairs with a .js argument that is rarely seen in benign workflows. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/007/ • https://cert.gov.ua/article/40240
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Bespoke Windows updater wrappers some sysadmins build using JScript
  • Vendor installers that pass --update to a side-by-side wscript helper
  • RMM tooling using JS-based updater payloads
  • Penetration test simulations referencing the same TTP
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"C:\Program Files\",@"C:\Program Files (x86)\") and InitiatingProcessFileName !endswith "explorer.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Resolve the full .js path from ProcessCommandLine — confirm whether it sits in a user-writable directory (Desktop, Downloads, Temp, %AppData%) which is the FrostyNeighbor pattern. Hash the .js and compare to ESET's published 8D1F2A6DF51C7783F2EAF1A0FC0FF8D032E5B57F. Step 2 (contain): Kill the wscript/cscript process tree; quarantine the .js; isolate host. Step 3 (hunt): Look for the parent process — the original execution should be either explorer.exe (manual double-click) or winrar.exe/7z.exe extracting from 53_7.03.2026_R.rar. Also hunt for the WinDataScope drop and outbound DNS to needbinding.icu / nebao.icu.

| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

FrostyNeighbor C2 callout to needbinding/nebao/algsat/sardk/alexavegas/lavanille AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS or HTTP egress to the six FrostyNeighbor C2 domains published by ESET in May 2026 (PicassoLoader on five .icu hosts plus a .buzz Cobalt Strike host). All six share the same actor infrastructure cluster registered between 2026-03-10 and 2026-04-14. Rationale: ESET published the full domain list in Table 2 of the article alongside first-seen dates from a freshly-registered actor infrastructure cluster (.icu/.buzz, no legitimate corporate use). Any host in a UA/PL/LT/EE government estate touching these domains is high-fidelity actor traffic. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1010/ • https://cert.gov.ua/article/40240
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DFIR team detonating samples in a connected analysis VM
  • Threat-intel ingestion proxies fetching the same samples
  • Researcher accessing the article and clicking through to defang links
  • Honeypot connecting to the C2 to fingerprint it
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has @"\Defender\")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the contacting process via InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName — for wscript.exe/cscript.exe parents this is almost certainly PicassoLoader. Capture the User-Agent and full URL. Step 2 (contain): Sinkhole the domain at egress (block at firewall + DNS); isolate the host; pull memory and disk image. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the resolved IP — Cloudflare-fronted but the origin may rotate; check for sibling domains on the same naming pattern (*-*.needbinding.icu, attachment-storage-asset-static.needbinding.icu), and hunt for the WinDataScope drop and ViberPC.dll on every host that resolved any of the six domains.
let FrostyDomains = dynamic(["needbinding.icu","nebao.icu","algsat.icu","alexavegas.icu","sardk.icu","lavanille.buzz"]);
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where RemoteUrl has_any (FrostyDomains)
    | extend Source="NetworkEvent"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source;
let EventHits = DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where ActionType =~ "DnsQueryResponse"
    | extend QueriedDomain = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).DnsQueryString)
    | where QueriedDomain has_any (FrostyDomains)
    | extend Source="DnsQuery"
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP="", RemoteUrl=QueriedDomain,
              RemotePort=tolong(0),
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessAccountName=AccountName, Source;
union NetHits, EventHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let FrostyDomains = dynamic(["needbinding.icu","nebao.icu","algsat.icu","alexavegas.icu","sardk.icu","lavanille.buzz"]);
union isfuzzy=true
    (ImDnsActivity
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
        | where DnsQuery has_any (FrostyDomains)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Domain=DnsQuery, Source="DNS"),
    (ImWebSession
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
        | where Url has_any (FrostyDomains) or HttpHostName has_any (FrostyDomains)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Domain=coalesce(HttpHostName,Url), Source="HTTP"),
    (CommonSecurityLog
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
        | where RequestURL has_any (FrostyDomains) or DestinationHostName has_any (FrostyDomains)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname=SourceHostName, SrcIpAddr=SourceIP, SrcUsername=SourceUserName, Domain=coalesce(DestinationHostName,RequestURL), Source="FW")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PicassoLoader scheduled-task creation by wscript/cscript after C2 XML fetch AIInstallation Medium
Detects FrostyNeighbor's persistence step: the JavaScript dropper downloads a scheduled-task XML template (served via the misleading Content-Type/Content-Disposition response to a .jpg URL) and then registers it. The parent-child chain of WSH spawning schtasks.exe or powershell.exe Register-ScheduledTask is article-specific. Rationale: The article describes the script downloading 'https://book-happy.needbinding[.]icu/wp-content/uploads/2023/10/1GreenAM.jpg' (which actually returns config.xml with Content-Type: application/xml) and then using it for persistence. Wscript/cscript spawning schtasks /Create /XML is a tight, low-FP pivot specific to this WSH-driven persistence pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/ • https://cert.gov.ua/article/40240
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Adobe / vendor installer JScript wrappers that schedule a maintenance task
  • Internal MDM scripts that register update tasks via JScript bootstrappers
  • Application Compatibility scripts during corporate imaging
  • RMM agents using a JScript first-stage that registers a service-task
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"C:\Program Files\",@"C:\Program Files (x86)\",@"C:\Windows\CCM\",@"C:\Windows\System32\GroupPolicy\") and AccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Dump the scheduled-task XML (schtasks /Query /TN <task> /XML) — the FrostyNeighbor template launches %AppData%\WinDataScope\Update.js on a schedule. Capture parent process tree back to the original .js file under the user profile. Step 2 (contain): schtasks /Delete /TN <task> /F; remove the WinDataScope folder; isolate host; pull memory. Step 3 (hunt): Across the org, look for any scheduled task whose Action.Command points into %AppData%\WinDataScope or whose RegistrationInfo.Source mentions WinDataScope; cross-reference with DNS hits on the six C2 domains.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/Create","/XML"))
      or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "Register-ScheduledTask")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
          ChildProcess=FileName, ChildCmd=ProcessCommandLine,
          ParentProcess=InitiatingProcessFileName,
          ParentCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          GrandparentProcess=InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate

| where (ActingProcessName has "schtasks.exe" and ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("/Create","/XML"))

title: WSH-Initiated Scheduled Task Registration (FrostyNeighbor PicassoLoader)
id: 2c8f47a3-9b14-4ee5-b87e-91a4f5d63c11
description: Detects wscript.exe or cscript.exe spawning schtasks.exe /Create /XML or powershell Register-ScheduledTask. This is the persistence step in FrostyNeighbor's March 2026 PicassoLoader chain, in which an XML template is downloaded under a fake .jpg URL and registered as a scheduled task.
references:
  - https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/frostyneighbor-fresh-mischief-digital-shenanigans/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/19
tags:
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.t1059.007
  - attack.persistence
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
  child_schtasks:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/Create'
      - '/XML'
  child_pwsh:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
    CommandLine|contains: 'Register-ScheduledTask'
  condition: parent and (child_schtasks or child_pwsh)
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate vendor installers that use JScript wrappers to register tasks (rare)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@ParentImage:(*\\wscript.exe OR *\\cscript.exe OR *\\WScript.exe OR *\\CScript.exe OR *\\WSCRIPT.EXE OR *\\CSCRIPT.EXE)) ((@Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SchTasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE) AND @CommandLine:(*/Create* OR */XML*)) OR (@Image:(*\\powershell.exe OR *\\PowerShell.exe OR *\\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\\pwsh.exe) AND @CommandLine:*Register-ScheduledTask*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i
| (ImageFileName=/schtasks\.exe$/i AND regex("(/Create|/XML)", field=CommandLine))
  OR (ImageFileName=/(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i AND regex("Register-ScheduledTask", field=CommandLine))
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())

FrostyNeighbor Cobalt Strike beacon ViberPC.dll image load AIInstallation Medium
Detects loading of ViberPC.dll, the final-stage Cobalt Strike beacon FrostyNeighbor masquerades as the legitimate Viber desktop messenger DLL. ESET publishes a SHA-1 (43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB) and the file is expected outside the legitimate Viber install path under the standard Cobalt Strike beacon naming pattern Win32/CobaltStrike.Beacon.S. Rationale: ESET published the exact SHA-1 (43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB) for the ViberPC.dll Cobalt Strike beacon in Table 1, classified Win32/CobaltStrike.Beacon.S. Combined with masquerading detection — ViberPC.dll loaded from a non-Viber path — this is a high-confidence final-stage beacon detection. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S0154/ • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1010/ • https://cert.gov.ua/article/40240
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1055.001 T1588.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Viber portable install on a corporate device outside standard install paths
  • DFIR / red-team Cobalt Strike training exercise with renamed loader
  • Backup software restoring a snapshot containing the IOC
  • File-server hosting a software repository with the sample present
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\Viber\",@"\Program Files (x86)\Viber\",@"\AppData\Local\Viber\") and SHA1 !in~ ("43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Hash-verify the loaded DLL against ESET's published SHA-1; capture the loading process (often rundll32.exe, regsvr32.exe, or a sacrificial process injected by PicassoLoader). Pull memory of the loading process for beacon config extraction. Step 2 (contain): Isolate host via EDR; block hash org-wide; sinkhole nama-belakang.nebao.icu and best-seller.lavanille.buzz at egress. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep all hosts for ViberPC.dll outside the Viber install path; pivot on beacon C2 IP after extracting the malleable profile; check AAD/SigninLogs for anomalous interactive logons from any host that loaded the beacon (lateral-movement indicator).
let FrostyHashes = dynamic(["43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB"]);
let ImageLoads = DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where FileName =~ "ViberPC.dll"
    | where SHA1 in~ (FrostyHashes)
         or not (FolderPath has @"\Viber\" or FolderPath has @"\Program Files\Viber")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
              InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="ImageLoad";
let FileWrites = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(60d)
    | where FileName =~ "ViberPC.dll"
    | where SHA1 in~ (FrostyHashes)
         or not (FolderPath has @"\Viber\" or FolderPath has @"\Program Files\Viber")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256,
              InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
              InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="FileWrite";
union ImageLoads, FileWrites
| order by Timestamp desc
let FrostyHashes = dynamic(["43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(60d)
| where TargetFileName =~ "ViberPC.dll"
| where TargetFileSHA1 in~ (FrostyHashes)
     or not (TargetFilePath has @"\Viber\" or TargetFilePath has @"\Program Files\Viber")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath,
          TargetFileSHA1, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject

         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    [| tstats `summariesonly` count

        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user

    [| tstats summariesonly=false count

    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("776A43E46C36A539C916ED426745EE96E2392B39", "8D1F2A6DF51C7783F2EAF1A0FC0FF8D032E5B57F", "B65551D339AECE718EA1465BF3542C794C445EFC", "43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB") or SHA1 in~ ("776A43E46C36A539C916ED426745EE96E2392B39", "8D1F2A6DF51C7783F2EAF1A0FC0FF8D032E5B57F", "B65551D339AECE718EA1465BF3542C794C445EFC", "43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB") or MD5 in~ ("776A43E46C36A539C916ED426745EE96E2392B39", "8D1F2A6DF51C7783F2EAF1A0FC0FF8D032E5B57F", "B65551D339AECE718EA1465BF3542C794C445EFC", "43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("776A43E46C36A539C916ED426745EE96E2392B39", "8D1F2A6DF51C7783F2EAF1A0FC0FF8D032E5B57F", "B65551D339AECE718EA1465BF3542C794C445EFC", "43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB") or SHA1 in~ ("776A43E46C36A539C916ED426745EE96E2392B39", "8D1F2A6DF51C7783F2EAF1A0FC0FF8D032E5B57F", "B65551D339AECE718EA1465BF3542C794C445EFC", "43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB") or MD5 in~ ("776A43E46C36A539C916ED426745EE96E2392B39", "8D1F2A6DF51C7783F2EAF1A0FC0FF8D032E5B57F", "B65551D339AECE718EA1465BF3542C794C445EFC", "43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["776A43E46C36A539C916ED426745EE96E2392B39", "8D1F2A6DF51C7783F2EAF1A0FC0FF8D032E5B57F", "B65551D339AECE718EA1465BF3542C794C445EFC", "43E30BE82D82B24A6496F6943ECB6877E83F88AB"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Mini Shai-Hulud dead-drop git commit authored as claude@users.noreply.github.com · [LLM] Node/npm/Bun process enumerating cloud, wallet, AI, and messaging credential file paths · Crypto-wallet file/keystore access by non-wallet process · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Mini Shai-Hulud npm Worm C2 callback to Session Protocol CDN and masscan.cloud AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS resolution or outbound TCP/UDP to the Session Protocol seed nodes (seed1.getsession.org, filev2.getsession.org) and api.masscan.cloud used by TeamPCP's Mini Shai-Hulud worm to exfiltrate harvested CI/CD secrets and developer credentials. These hostnames are not part of any legitimate enterprise software supply chain and any contact is high-fidelity. Rationale: Domains seed1.getsession.org, filev2.getsession.org, and api.masscan.cloud are named explicitly as the worm's exfiltration channel in the StepSecurity write-up. Session Protocol nodes have zero legitimate enterprise use and api.masscan.cloud is the same C2 infrastructure observed across the @antv variant (memory observation 1252) — high-fidelity primary IOCs across multiple StepSecurity / Socket.dev / JFrog reports on the campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1567/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1071/001/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567 T1568
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer running the Session Messenger desktop app on a corp workstation (rare; whitelist by user)
  • Security researchers detonating the worm in an authorized sandbox host
  • Internal red team replaying campaign IOCs during a purple-team exercise
  • Threat-intel platforms (MISP, OpenCTI) performing connectivity checks against indicator URLs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("session.exe","Session.exe") and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("session.exe","Session.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Identify the InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName — confirm it is node, npm, bun, git, or a CI runner process (and not Session Messenger). Pivot on DeviceId to list every package install in the prior 24h on that host. Step 2 (Contain): Isolate the device via Defender Live Response, force-rotate all credentials in scope (npm tokens, GitHub PATs, cloud keys, .env values), and revoke OIDC trust on the affected GitHub Actions repo. Step 3 (Hunt): Across the org, sweep DeviceFileEvents for router_init.js drops and DeviceProcessEvents for any commit authored as claude@users.noreply.github.com in the last 14d to find every laterally-infected publisher.
let CampaignHosts = dynamic(["seed1.getsession.org","filev2.getsession.org","api.masscan.cloud"]);
let NetHits = DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl has_any (CampaignHosts) or tostring(parse_url(RemoteUrl).Host) in~ (CampaignHosts)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountUpn=InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, Indicator=coalesce(RemoteUrl, RemoteIP), Source="network", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName;
let EvHits = DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType in ("DnsQueryResponse","ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionFailed","NetworkConnectionEvents")
  | where RemoteUrl has_any (CampaignHosts) or AdditionalFields has_any (CampaignHosts)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountUpn=InitiatingProcessAccountUpn, Indicator=coalesce(RemoteUrl, tostring(AdditionalFields)), Source="device-event", InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName=tostring(parse_json(""));
NetHits
| union EvHits
| order by Timestamp desc
let CampaignHosts = dynamic(["seed1.getsession.org","filev2.getsession.org","api.masscan.cloud"]);
let DnsHits = DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Name has_any (CampaignHosts)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Indicator=Name, Source="DnsEvents";
let AsimDns = ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DnsQuery has_any (CampaignHosts)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, Indicator=DnsQuery, Source="ImDnsActivity";
let ProxyHits = CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationHostName has_any (CampaignHosts) or RequestURL has_any (CampaignHosts)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, Indicator=coalesce(DestinationHostName, RequestURL), Source="Proxy/CEF";
let WebHits = ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where HttpHostName has_any (CampaignHosts) or Url has_any (CampaignHosts)
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, Indicator=coalesce(HttpHostName, Url), Source="ImWebSession";
DnsHits | union AsimDns, ProxyHits, WebHits
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by Computer, ClientIP, Indicator, Source
| order by LastSeen desc
title: Mini Shai-Hulud npm Worm C2 to Session Protocol and masscan.cloud
id: 7e3a8e1c-1b6f-4f8e-9c2a-5a8f8d2c4ac1
description: Detects DNS query or network connection to TeamPCP Mini Shai-Hulud exfiltration infrastructure (Session Protocol seed/file nodes and api.masscan.cloud).
references:

  category: dns

    QueryName:
      - 'seed1.getsession.org'
      - 'filev2.getsession.org'

falsepositives:

level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR linux.auditd OR linux.syslog) ((@EventID:22 AND (@QueryName:seed1.getsession.org OR @QueryName:filev2.getsession.org OR @QueryName:api.masscan.cloud)) OR (@EventID:3 AND (@DestinationHostname:seed1.getsession.org OR @DestinationHostname:filev2.getsession.org OR @DestinationHostname:api.masscan.cloud)) OR @network.destination.domain:(seed1.getsession.org OR filev2.getsession.org OR api.masscan.cloud))

| (DomainName=/^(seed1\.getsession\.org|filev2\.getsession\.org|api\.masscan\.cloud)$/i OR RemoteAddressIP4=* AND ContextImageFileName=/(node|npm|bun|git)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, RemoteAddressIP4, ContextImageFileName, ContextProcessId], function=count())
| sort(_count, order=desc)

TeamPCP Mini Shai-Hulud stealer payload hash match (SHA256/SHA1) AIInstallation High
Alerts on disk-write or in-memory execution of a binary whose SHA256 or SHA1 matches the obfuscated 2.3 MB credential-stealer payload published by TeamPCP across @tanstack, @uipath, @draftlab and other compromised npm packages. The hashes are the cleanest single-source-of-truth IOCs in this campaign and are reused unchanged across all 50+ compromised package versions. Rationale: Four SHA256 and three SHA1 hashes were published in the StepSecurity article as the canonical fingerprint of the 2.3 MB obfuscated stealer payload. These hashes were observed unchanged across all listed @tanstack/@uipath/@draftlab versions and were corroborated in earlier @antv variant reporting (Socket.dev, JFrog, StepSecurity — memory observations 1249, 1250, 1252). Hash-based hunting carries zero ambiguity and zero FP risk against benign software. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized sandbox detonation by malware researchers on a forensic workstation
  • Internal threat-hunting team running yara/hash sweeps that touch the artifact during analysis
  • Backup or DLP product scanning a quarantined file and re-hashing it
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has "\\SandboxAnalysis\\" and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("yara.exe","yara64.exe","capa.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Pivot on DeviceId to the InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm the parent is npm/node/bun/yarn, then enumerate which package and version installed (look in npm-cache or package-lock.json on the host). Step 2 (Contain): Isolate host, kill node/bun processes, force-rotate every credential reachable from that machine (npm tokens, GH PATs, cloud keys, AI tool keys, wallets, messaging app tokens), revoke any OIDC trust the host's CI runner role had. Step 3 (Hunt): Sweep org for the file hash on every host AND query DeviceFileEvents for any router_init.js drop in node_modules in the last 30d to find lateral worm spread.

let StealerSha1 = dynamic(["79ac49eedf774dd4b0cfa308722bc463cfe5885c","de0fac2e4500dabe0009e67214ff5f5447ce83dd","bbbca2ddaa5d8feaa63e36b76fdaad77386f024f"]);
let ProcHits = DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where SHA256 in~ (StealerSha256) or SHA1 in~ (StealerSha1) or InitiatingProcessSHA256 in~ (StealerSha256) or InitiatingProcessSHA1 in~ (StealerSha1)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, Source="DeviceProcessEvents";

Mini Shai-Hulud router_init.js dropped at npm package root in node_modules AIInstallation High
Detects file writes of a router_init.js file directly at a package root inside node_modules with a size > 1 MB on a single line — the exact filesystem signature documented in the StepSecurity comparison of clean (1.166.42) vs compromised (1.166.48) @tanstack tarballs (2,341,681 bytes, single line). Catches the worm at install time before the preinstall payload executes. Rationale: Table 2 in the article (Clean 1.166.42 vs Compromised 1.166.48) explicitly identifies router_init.js at root, 2,341,681 bytes, single line, as the structural marker of every compromised tarball. The file is absent from clean versions and is the worm's first-stage loader — file create from npm/node into node_modules is the exact moment of compromise. Cross-checked against the @antv variant analysis (memory observation 1247) which also noted the same loader file pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/002/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1027 T1546
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate package coincidentally shipping a router_init.js at root (validate by hash — non-stealer hash + size != 2.3 MB single-line is FP)
  • Internal monorepo with a custom build step that generates router_init.js under node_modules cache
  • Developer extracting/inspecting the malicious tarball in a sandbox without executing
Suppression filter
| where SHA256 in~ ("ab4fcadaec49c03278063dd269ea5eef82d24f2124a8e15d7b90f2fa8601266c","0c0e873033875f1bc471eda37e3b9d0f9b89bd41a4bbb4f86746caa2176c40aa","2ec78d556d696e208927cc503d48e4b5eb56b31abc2870c2ed2e98d6be27fc96","7c12d8614c624c70d6dd6fc2ee289332474abaa38f70ebe2cdef064923ca3a9b") or FileSize between (2000000 .. 3500000)
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Capture SHA256 of the file and compare against the four known stealer hashes; check the package.json and package-lock.json in the parent directory to identify which compromised package landed on disk. Step 2 (Contain): Quarantine host, kill node processes, remove the node_modules tree, force-rotate any tokens stored in npm/git config on the host (npm tokens, GitHub PATs, ~/.aws/credentials, wallet seeds). Step 3 (Hunt): Search org for all npm publish events in last 30d from this user/runner identity AND for any GitHub commit authored as claude@users.noreply.github.com to find onward worm spread.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed")
| where FileName =~ "router_init.js"
| where FolderPath has "node_modules"
| where FileSize > 1000000  // clean tarball baseline is no router_init.js; compromised version is ~2.3MB single line
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","npm","node","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","bun.exe","bun","corepack.exe")
   or InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("node.exe","npm.exe","pnpm.exe","yarn.exe","bun.exe","corepack.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, FileSize, SHA256,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileCreate","FileRenamed")
| where TargetFileName =~ "router_init.js"
| where TargetFilePath has "node_modules"
| where TargetFileSize > 1000000
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("node","npm","pnpm","yarn","bun","corepack")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSize, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Mini Shai-Hulud router_init.js Drop in npm node_modules
id: a1c9d3e2-8a5d-4f1c-9d2e-1a8b3c5d7e09
description: Detects creation of router_init.js inside a node_modules tree by an npm/node/pnpm/yarn/bun process — TeamPCP's worm signature.
references:
  - https://www.stepsecurity.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-is-back-a-self-spreading-supply-chain-attack-hits-the-npm-ecosystem
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/05/20
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1195.002
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_file:
    TargetFilename|endswith: '\router_init.js'
    TargetFilename|contains: '\node_modules\'
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\node.exe'
      - '\npm.exe'
      - '\pnpm.exe'
      - '\yarn.exe'
      - '\bun.exe'
      - '\corepack.exe'
  condition: selection_file and selection_proc
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate npm package that ships a top-level router_init.js (verify by hash against the four known stealer SHA256s before suppressing)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @TargetFilename:(*\\node_modules\\*\\router_init.js OR *\\node_modules\\*\\Router_Init.js OR *\\node_modules\\*\\ROUTER_INIT.JS OR */node_modules/*/router_init.js) @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\npm.exe OR *\\pnpm.exe OR *\\yarn.exe OR *\\bun.exe OR */bin/node OR */bin/npm)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/[\\\/]node_modules[\\\/].*[\\\/]router_init\.js$/i
| WrittenBytes>1000000
| ContextImageFileName=/(node|npm|pnpm|yarn|bun|corepack)\.exe$/i OR ContextImageFileName=/\/(node|npm|pnpm|yarn|bun|corepack)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, TargetFileName, ContextImageFileName, WrittenBytes], function=count())
| sort(_count, order=desc)
